1. **Chart type**  
   Multi-series **line chart**.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - No faceting or small multiples  
   - Multiple series overlaid in a single panel  
   - Differentiation by **color** (school level) and **line style/marker style** (product type: solid vs dotted)

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Percent of students | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| School level (High school, Middle school) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (orange vs blue), direct text labels at line ends |
| Tobacco product category (Any tobacco product, E-cigarettes) | Categorical/nominal | Line style/series distinction (solid vs dotted), direct text labels near lines |

**Visible series:**  
- High school — Any tobacco product  
- High school — E-cigarettes  
- Middle school — Any tobacco product  
- Middle school — E-cigarettes

comments.raw_comment: Researchers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have collected data on the consumption of tobacco products by middle school and high school students from 2011-2018. This information is displayed in the graph to the left, and there are two distinct lines per age group, one regarding tobacco products at large, and the other specifically concerning e-cigarettes. I notice that while the use of any tobacco products has increased for middle schoolers in 2017 from roughly 4% to 7% of students, the use of any tobacco products for high schoolers has significantly jumped in 2017 from about 19% to about 27% of students. I see that the line describing the use of exclusively e-cigarettes is identical to the upward trend of the line depicting the use of any tobacco product, which makes me thinks that e-cigarettes are the major contributor to the growth in consumption over the past seven years. Perhaps this is the obvious question, but I wonder why this is? I have a hard time coming to any solid answer to this question. Also, what could the government do to deter the continuation of this pattern? A month ago, I heard in the news that the FDA is working on banning popular flavors of pods for Juuls, a very popular e-cigarette brand, that students might find appealing, such as mango and mint. How else could the government aid this situation? Is the federal government’s intervention constitutional?

comments.raw_comment: When I looked at the graph, I noticed that about 25% of high school students were using tobacco products. This was shown at a consistent rate of about 25% between the years 2011 to 2013. For E-cigarettes, the rate of use was at about 2% between the years 2011 to 2013. Suddenly the use of E-cigarettes increased greatly around 2013, and the use for tobacco products plummeted. I can assume that for whatever reason, E-cigarettes were highly marketed and almost replaced tobacco-related products. E-cigarettes were possibly marketed as the healthier option which led young consumers to try it for themselves. The data for middle schoolers showed the same results as the high school data, but tobacco products stayed with consistent use at about 8%. E-cigarettes then jumped from 1% use and slowly started inclining in 2013. With both data though, E-cigarette use starts to go down in 2015. This is probably because of new findings of all the chemicals that turned young consumers away.  In 2017, both graphs experienced a great increase. I think this was because of increasing popularity with E-cigarette brands such as the Juul. A title for this graph may be "E-Cigarettes Are on the Rise, But Why?"

comments.raw_comment: By looking at the graph, I noticed a few key features. First, I saw that there is a large jump between the amount of middle school aged adolescents who have used tobacco products and high school aged adolescents who have used tobacco products. Second, I noticed that the prevalence of the use of E-cigarettes was quite low, until 2013, where a considerable jump occurs. Third, I noticed that the lines for any tobacco products, in both middle and high school aged adolescents, continue with seemingly no change before 2011, indicating that tobacco products, like cigarettes, had been used by students before the graph starts. I wonder about what other tobacco products have been recorded in the making of this graph. I also wonder how accurate the data really is, considering may students may lie about what tobacco products they have used. The story this graph is telling is that, after some fluctuations, E-cigarette and overall tobacco use is currently rising among adolescents. My headline to accompany this graph would be, "Tobacco Gets a New Disguise in E-Cigarettes!" This title, which doubles as a claim, is supported by the fact that tobacco use has recently decreased in products other than E-cigarettes (You can tell because the distance between the solid and dotted lines has recently decreased), but overall has gone up.

comments.raw_comment: I notice that "juul" is not specifically included in this graph. As a teenager, nearly ending high school, I can not say that most of my peers partake in smoking cigarettes or e-cigarettes. Of course, I can not speak for the whole of the country, but don't the Center for Disease Control and Prevention and the FDA serve under similar departments? Both in the Department of Health and Human Services- shouldn't they be in communication with one another, discussing the "juul" epidemic/fanfare? So, I wonder why "juul" was not included in this graph, and where that line would lie. Considering the FDA recently banned mango pods from being distributed aside from what has already been produced, I feel like is a pertinent addition to the graph. Perhaps the author of this graph wanted to show that any tobacco product- such as Juul or chewing tobacco- surpasses e-cigarettes. 25% of high school students partake in some sort of tobacco product, while about 8% do so in middle school. I wonder if the creator of this graph realizes the effect of Juul. A catchy phrase for this graph could be, "The perpetrator who shall not be named".

comments.raw_comment: Vaping: One of the most prominent epidemics among teenagers. I was almost waiting for a graph about it to appear on this site. This graph calculates the percentage of students in both middle school and high school that have used any tobacco product versus e-cigarettes. My eye is immediately drawn to the E-cigarette uprising. The number of high school students using e-cigarettes, or "juuls", has increased from about 2% to about 21% from 2011-2018. Additionally, the middle school percantage of e-cigarette users has increased by about 5%. This statistic does NOT surprise me. I've seen so many teenagers around me vaping, and it's sad as they soon become addicted to nicotine. Teenagers don't realize that though they may look "cool" or impress their peers, they are placing themselves on a dangerous path. Other tobacco products have been on a steady pace for middle schoolers at around 8%. High schoolers, on the other hand, appear to have stopped using Tobacco products between 2016-2017. However, they are now on the rise again with about 27% of students using them. Though we are unsure of the health risks that new tobacco technology entails, we know that it is not good for us. However, the companies that sell them are certainly having a good time.

Today’s graph shows tobacco consumption among students for 2011 - 2018.  What do we notice and wonder about e-cigarettes?
From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, give us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  
Plus, please have your students share with us a catchy headline that captures your ideas about the graph. 
On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
(The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be released tomorrow, Thursday, March 7 with moderation on Wednesday, March 13.  The topic:  Electricity.)
